title: SERF: A Schema-Guided Evidence Retrieval Framework for Token-Efficient Structured Data Extraction from Scientific Literature
content: Scientific literature contains rich experimental knowledge, but much of it remains embedded in unstructured PDFs, tables, figures, captions, and narrative text. Direct full-document prompting with large language models introduces excessive context, increasing token usage and weakening evidence traceability for structured extraction. This paper presents SERF, a Schema-guided Evidence Retrieval Framework for token-efficient structured data extraction from scientific literature. The framework parses scientific PDFs into section-aware semantic chunks, constructs a document-aware vocabulary to reduce terminology mismatch, and applies LLM-based query adaptation to expand schema field guides with source-specific aliases. The adapted guides then drive Bi-Encoder retrieval and Cross-Encoder reranking to select compact evidence for schema-constrained JSON generation. To improve completeness, SERF applies Section-Mapped Iterative Refilling, which recovers missing fields by searching likely source sections instead of reprocessing the full document. We evaluate SERF from both retrieval quality and end-to-end extraction quality. On PubMed RCT, a large sentence-level scientific abstract benchmark, SERF achieves stronger macro-level retrieval balance, demonstrating the effectiveness of two-stage schema-guided evidence selection. Field-wise results further show that SERF is effective at retrieving introductory, methodological, result-oriented, and conclusion-oriented evidence. In a domain-specific full-text extraction setting, SERF reduces average input tokens by 37% compared with full-document prompting while maintaining comparable completeness and matching judge-based precision. Compared with external extraction baselines, SERF achieves a better balance between token efficiency, extraction quality, and evidence traceability. These results show that SERF is an effective token-efficient procedure to convert unstructured scientific papers into standardized and machine-readable records while preserving compact and verifiable evidence support.
